thesis: Taxation was always sold as temporary, but every single time, it became permanent — and the same human dynamics that made it necessary are why it never went away.
hook: Around 3000 BCE, Egyptian pharaohs invented taxation by taking a 20 percent cut of your grain harvest — and they called it a temporary emergency measure to build pyramids.
stakes: If the most coercive institution in human history was born from a promise its founders never intended to keep, you should probably read that tax bill a little more carefully.
counterpoint: Some economists argue that complex societies require taxation to function, and that the permanence of taxes reflects their genuine necessity rather than government overreach.
implication: The next time someone tells you a new tax is temporary, you have 5,000 years of receipts saying otherwise — and the structure of who collects, who pays, and who benefits hasn't really changed.
close: The sesh per hedj beat farmers who couldn't pay. The publicani extracted blood. And every time the system got so brutal that people revolted and revenue collapsed, they replaced it with something that looked cleaner — but still took 20 percent. Your grain, your blood, your attention. Pay attention to what they're calling temporary. It won't be.
